title: When Less is More - Minimalism in Table Top Adventure Games
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9rJgQmuc2SM

Daniel (@dungeondive) makes the case for restraint, sorting minimalism in adventure games into three kinds — artistic, component, and mechanical — and pulling an example off his shelf for each. He loves the maximalist icons (Arkham Horror, Eldritch Horror, Shadows of Brimstone), but concedes their bulk is a barrier: hard to store, slow to the table. The counterexamples do more with less. The Adventure of D (Jack D Games) squeezes a full crawl into a Magic-starter-sized box through multi-use cards. Seven Moons and Glory: Second Edition strip an adventure game to the bare minimum and lose nothing — take one piece away from Glory, Daniel says, and it stops being a game. Shadows of Malice (Devious Weasel) leans into artistic minimalism: placeholder art the playtesters refused to give up, almost no flavour text, and a creature generator that hands worldbuilding to your imagination. Darkest Night shows mechanical minimalism can strengthen theme — one action per turn makes sneaking past the necromancer feel genuinely furtive. Dragons Down carries zero flavour text, so every story is one you author at the table. And the game that sparked the topic, Tom Wham's Search for the Emperor's Treasure, nails all three with two-minute turns and doodle charm. Sometimes the smallest game is exactly the one you want.

----

Which do you reach for more often — a maximalist box stuffed with variety, or a minimalist game that hits the table in minutes? And has a stripped-down design ever given you a *better* story than a script-heavy campaign?
